title: The Long-Term Memory Problem: Why Teaching and Learning Policies Fail 14, 2025
author: Adam Boxer
summary: Adam Boxer returns to his 'Schoolington Academy' framing device to diagnose a different problem than his autonomy piece: a school with a well-designed, well-followed Teaching and Learning policy -- including a retrieval-based Do Now -- whose outcomes still aren't improving. Where classroom observation shows strong alignment between policy and practice, Boxer's investigative move is asking individual students basic recall questions from lessons taught just three weeks earlier; across subjects and year groups, students overwhelmingly cannot answer them, revealing that in-the-moment teaching quality has decoupled entirely from long-term retention. He catalogues why schools systematically under-invest in genuine long-term memory strategy: a historic disciplinary bias against knowledge-focused teaching that is only slowly reversing, the fact that long-term learning is inherently harder to observe than short-term proxies like behaviour or feedback delivery, curriculum time pressure that crowds out consolidation, the simple discomfort of confronting how much students forget, the planning complexity of spacing and sequencing retrieval questions, and schools' tendency to over-rely on a superficial 'Do Now' fix or offload the problem entirely to homework that gets 'set and forget' treatment. Boxer's conclusion is that without a deliberate, planned, curriculum-wide strategy for retrieval over time, no amount of excellent in-the-moment teaching can compensate, and he poses four concrete planning questions for school leaders to answer.
points: Boxer's diagnostic method is the article's strongest evidence: asking individual students basic recall questions from a lesson taught three weeks prior, across subjects and year groups, and finding they 'cannot answer the questions' in almost all cases -- despite classroom practice matching policy.

His central claim decouples two things schools often conflate: quality of in-the-moment teaching (which Schoolington has) and a genuine strategy for long-term retention over time (which it lacks) -- excellence in one doesn't guarantee the other.

He identifies 'set and forget' homework as a specific failure mode: schools offload retrieval practice to homework assuming it solves the time problem, but teachers rarely give feedback on it or use it to adapt lessons, silently communicating to students that it doesn't matter.

Boxer names Coe's 'proxies for learning' research as a mechanism explaining why schools miss this problem: long-term retention is harder to observe than surface indicators like student behaviour or busyness, so schools latch onto what's visible rather than what matters.

His closing planning questions reframe the problem as a leadership responsibility, not a teacher-level fix: has the curriculum been codified for retrieval, is delivery timed and sequenced, and is there a strategy for increasing quality retrieval at home.
quotes: I quietly ask a student if I can borrow their exercise book. I leaf back to a lesson from three weeks ago, and ask the student a couple of basic recall questions about that lesson’s content. They cannot answer the questions.

However well designed our lessons, however clear our explanations, however thorough our checks for understanding and however extensive our independent practice: without a clear strategy for how students are going to remember it over the long term, we are wasting our time.

Professor Coe’s seminal work on “proxies for learning” taught us that when trying to establish the quality of a teacher or lesson we latch onto things that are readily observable, like student behaviour, busy-ness, and if feedback is being delivered.
When teachers “set and forget” they therefore communicate that they don’t really care what students do, so long as they do it. But if the teacher doesn’t care, the students certainly won’t.

It is my belief that in many schools, the lack of a proper approach to long-term memory serves as a lead weight on outcomes. When students turn up to exams their knowledge is fragmented, idiosyncratic and cannot cohere into an expressible form.

We need to hold to one simple truth: if we have not adequately strategised for long-term learning, nothing we do in the class can compensate. We need to scrutinise our teaching and our leading and wonder: have we been looking in the wrong direction?
